lw42.argument: Option [2] ('It is therefore incumbent upon all prospective matriculants to apprehend the night's essential function') does drop the offhand 'Anyway' and 'pretty much' and is unmistakably purposeful, so a reader focused only on the first half of the stem might pick it. But the stem also requires 'a tone suited to a library's public blog,' and the passage's register ('folding chairs, a dented coffee urn,' 'Hope to see you there') is plain and conversational; the stilted diction is a mismatch. [1] makes a false promise, [3] is more offhand than the original.

Option [3] keeps both facts ('left high school at seventeen' and 'at forty-one he had just finished an associate degree at Calloway Valley') and is grammatically a single sentence, so a careless reader might accept it. However 'so' makes the degree a consequence of leaving high school, destroying the contrast the stem demands; 'but' in the key preserves it. [1] is a comma splice; [2] drops the early exit entirely.
lw42.stem_issue: The stem says to combine sentences 4 and 5, but every option (including the key) silently discards the second clause of sentence 5 ('he was trying to figure out which of his credits would count toward the nursing program at Ridgeline State University'), so none is a genuine combination of the two sentences; the task is really 'rewrite with contrast,' not 'combine.'

lw42.argument: Option [2] ('Our annual Transfer Night held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors') correctly separates weekday from date and closes the interrupter with a comma after '17'; a careless reader might miss that the opening comma before 'held' is absent, leaving the nonessential participial phrase only half set off. [0] misuses semicolons, [1] omits both the Thursday/April comma and the closing comma.
lw42.key_flaw: The keyed wording is identical to sentence 3 as it already appears in the passage ('Our annual Transfer Night, held this year on Thursday, April 17, brings advisors'). The stem implies there is a punctuation problem to fix, but there is none; the item tests nothing about revising the draft and the answer can be found by simply matching the passage text.
lw42.stem_issue: The sentence is already correctly punctuated in the passage, so the 'revision' premise is false and the item is trivial.

lw42.argument: Option [2] ('Parking is available behind the library, and the coffee urn will be refilled throughout the evening') echoes a concrete detail from sentence 1 ('a dented coffee urn') and offers practical, low-stakes information that could ease a nervous newcomer. But it never addresses the stated goal—reassuring people 'who are not sure they belong there'—whereas the key explicitly says 'there is a chair waiting for you, whatever your story.' [0] is slangy and over-hyped; [3] actively excludes the uncertain reader.

lr42.argument: The paragraph opens with and dwells on the niece's victory: 'built by her niece at the kitchen table while Lenore protested from the next room that she did not want her face on the internet. The niece won.' A reader might take this anecdote as the paragraph's organizing point, especially since paragraph 6 returns to it ('she hated being made an example of'). But it is only the first two sentences; the bulk of the paragraph catalogs what the money covered ('the share of dialysis the insurance would not, the gas... three months of rent') and the donors' affection ('you waited for me in the snow'), which paragraph 4 explicitly concedes ('the money was real, and so was the comfort'). Option [2] is contradicted by the text (the page 'covered' the costs), and [0] has no support—the notes express gratitude, not guilt.
lr42.key_flaw: The justification refers to 'the blueprint,' an internal authoring artifact not visible to test-takers; the key's clause 'so that the critique to come cannot be dismissed as ingratitude' is an inference supported by paragraph 4 rather than stated in paragraph 2, but it is a reasonable reading of the paragraph's function.

lr42.argument: The sentence immediately follows 'Lenore would have disliked this column; she hated being made an example of,' and the 'But' pivot could be read as the writer salvaging Lenore's implicit endorsement: her lifelong conduct ('she waited for every child') is offered as the real authority behind the column's demand. A careless reader might therefore see the sentence as reassuring readers that Lenore's own values back the argument. However, the writer never claims she would have endorsed it—he concedes the opposite—and instead converts her behavior into an 'instruction for the rest of us,' with 'the ones nobody else was watching for' clearly recalling Aurelio ('a man whom fewer people had met'). Options [0] and [1] have no textual basis: the sentence neither congratulates donors nor evokes fear for readers' own children.
lr42.stem_issue: The keyed option is noticeably longer and more elaborated than the three distractors (including an explanatory tail clause, 'so the demand feels like loyalty rather than rebuke'), which makes it stand out on length alone; the options are not fully parallel.
